name: Bhagavad Gita
info: The Bhagavad Gita is a Hindu scripture of 700 verses, part of the Mahabharata and likely composed in the second or first century BCE, in which Krishna advises the warrior Arjuna on duty, knowledge and devotion before the Kurukshetra War.

facts.made: Ascribed by tradition to the sage Vyasa; scholars regard it as a composite work of several authors or compilers
facts.form: A Sanskrit poem of 700 verses in 18 chapters, mostly in the anushtubh metre, set within the Bhishma Parva of the Mahabharata
facts.where: Manuscripts in many Indic scripts found on the Indian subcontinent, within the Mahabharata or on their own; the Gita manuscript was added to UNESCO's Memory of the World Register in April 2025
facts.known: The dialogue of Arjuna and Krishna on a battlefield; the teaching of selfless action; the three disciplines of knowledge, action and devotion; Krishna's universal form in chapter 11; commentaries by Shankara, Ramanuja and Madhvacharya; translations in many languages

t: The Gita is a dialogue between Arjuna and his charioteer Krishna, an avatar of Vishnu, at the start of the Kurukshetra War, and it forms part of the Mahabharata.
It brings together Vedic dharma, Sankhya-based yoga and knowledge, and bhakti (devotion), and teaches action without craving its fruits.
Tradition ascribes it to Vyasa, while scholars see a composite work, generally dated to the second or first century BCE, which has drawn hundreds of commentaries and readings.
dyk: Richard Davis cites a count by Callewaert and Hemraj in 1982 of 1,891 translations of the Bhagavad Gita in 75 languages, 273 of them in English.
ev: The Gita is generally dated to this time, though earlier and later estimates exist and 200 BCE may be the date of a major revision
Adi Shankara writes the oldest surviving commentary, which reads the text as teaching the non-dualism of Atman and Brahman
Ramanuja writes his Gita Bhashya, reading the text as qualified monism and Krishna's birth as physically real
Dnyaneshwar completes the Dnyaneshwari, a Marathi commentary and the oldest surviving literary work in that language
Charles Wilkins publishes the first English translation, with an introduction by Warren Hastings
Bal Gangadhar Tilak writes his commentary Shrimadh Bhagavad Gita Rahasya while serving a sentence for sedition
Gandhi's commentary, written in Gujarati in 1929 and translated by Mahadev Desai, is published in English
The Bhagavad Gita manuscript is added to UNESCO's Memory of the World Register

sections.origins:
The Bhagavad Gita (Sanskrit, literally 'God's song') is a Hindu scripture that forms part of the Mahabharata, in its sixth book, the Bhishma Parva. It is generally dated to the second or first century BCE, though a later estimate (1st century CE) and earlier ones (400 to 500 BCE) have been given, and 200 BCE may be the date of a major revision. Jeaneane Fowler writes that the dating depends in part on whether the Gita belonged to the early versions of the Mahabharata or was inserted later, and the epic was itself likely compiled over several hundred years.

Arthur Basham argues that the text belongs to an era when the ethics of war were questioned and renunciation was becoming popular, after the rise of Buddhism and Jainism in the 5th century BCE and the life of Ashoka in the 3rd, so that a first version may date from the 3rd century BCE or later. Winthrop Sargeant places its language, Epic-Puranic Sanskrit, after Panini but before the long compounds of classical Sanskrit. Kashi Nath Upadhyaya argues instead for the fifth or fourth century BCE.

Scholars describe it as a synthesis of Vedic dharma (duty), Sankhya-based yoga and jnana (knowledge), and bhakti, drawing on the Upanishads. Dennis Hudson proposes that the Gita and the Pancaratra Agama share Vasudeva-Krishna roots.
sections.content:
The Gita is a dialogue between the Pandava prince Arjuna and his charioteer Krishna, whom Hindu tradition regards as an avatar of Vishnu, just before the Kurukshetra War. Arjuna asks Krishna to drive to the centre of the battlefield between the two armies. Seeing relatives, friends and teachers among his enemies, he is filled with doubt and despair, drops his bow and wonders whether to renounce his duty. Sanjaya, counsellor of the Kuru king Dhritarashtra, acts as a secondary narrator, with Dhritarashtra as his audience.

The poem has 18 chapters and 700 verses. In chapter 2 Krishna begins the philosophy, teaching the eternal nature of the soul (atman) and the temporary nature of the body, and advising Arjuna to do his warrior duty with detachment. Chapter 3 treats karma yoga, action without craving its fruits. Chapter 11 shows Arjuna Krishna's universal form (Vishvarupa), chapter 12 praises devotion (bhakti), and chapter 14 explains the three gunas, sattva, rajas and tamas. Chapter 18, the longest at 78 verses, summarises the teaching: renunciation of the fruits of action and surrender to Krishna.

The text sets out three disciplines, jnana (knowledge), karma (action) and bhakti (devotion). Fowler states that it does not raise any of them to a status that excludes the others; what joins them is 'inner renunciation'. Some scholars treat meditation (raja yoga) as a fourth path.
sections.making:
Indian tradition ascribes the Gita, like the Mahabharata, to the sage Vyasa. A Hindu legend narrates that Vyasa composed it and that Ganesha broke off one of his tusks and used it to write the epic down. Scholars consider Vyasa a mythical or symbolic author, in part because the name is also a title for the compiler of a text, and tradition makes him the compiler of the Vedas and the Puranas too, texts dated about two millennia apart. Alexus McLeod holds it 'impossible to link the Bhagavad Gita to a single author', and Basham counts three or more authors or compilers, pointing to the discontinuous mixing of philosophical verses with passionately theistic ones.

J. A. B. van Buitenen finds the Gita so well knit into the Mahabharata that it was not an independent text that 'somehow wandered into the epic', but one conceived by the epic's authors to bring the dharmic dilemma of a war to a climax and solution. Basham cites chapter 5 as showing signs of interpolation: verses 5.23 to 5.28 give the sage's goal as the impersonal Brahman, while verse 5.29 gives it as the personal God Krishna.

The verses are mostly in the anushtubh metre, in which each shloka is a couplet of two quarters of eight syllables; at dramatic moments the text uses the tristubh metre of the Vedas, with eleven syllables to a quarter.
sections.reception:
Commentary on the Gita is old and abundant: some 227 commentaries survive in Sanskrit alone, and Mysore Hiriyanna calls it 'one of the hardest books to interpret'. Adi Shankara's commentary (c. 800 CE), the oldest surviving and most influential, reads it as teaching the non-dualism of Atman and Brahman and treats bhakti as a practice that purifies the mind. Ramanuja, in the 11th and early 12th centuries, read it as qualified monism (Vishishtadvaita) and identified the supreme Brahman with Narayana, or Vishnu. Madhvacharya (c. 1250) held that the individual soul, Vishnu and the world are fundamentally different. Abhinavagupta wrote in the Kashmir Shaiva tradition, and Dnyaneshwar wrote in Marathi in the 13th century. Chaitanya's followers used the Gita and the Bhagavata Purana as the school's primary scriptural sources.

Catherine Robinson notes that scholars increasingly recognise the Gita's extraordinary prominence as a feature of modernity. Eric Sharpe dates the change to the 1880s and after 1900, Arvind Sharma to the 1920s. Gerald James Larson writes that if any one text comes near to embodying the totality of what it is to be a Hindu, it is the Bhagavad Gita.

Readers disagree about it. B. R. Ambedkar criticised its stance on caste and called its defence of killing unethical, while Gandhi credited his commitment to ahimsa (non-violence) to the Gita, and Lala Lajpat Rai and Tilak read it as defending war when necessary.
sections.survival:
The Gita is preserved within the Bhishma Parva of the Mahabharata, numbered as chapters 6.23 to 6.40 or 6.25 to 6.42 depending on the recension. It is also often kept and studied on its own, with its chapters renumbered 1 to 18. Its manuscripts exist in numerous Indic scripts, among them the now dormant Sharada script. Unlike the large variations in the rest of the Mahabharata manuscripts, the Gita manuscripts show only minor variations, though alternate versions exist, such as one found in Kashmir, and Abhinavagupta commented on a slightly different recension from Shankara's. Gambhirananda suggests that old manuscripts may have had 745 verses, but no such manuscript has been found; Shankara stated that the Gita has 700, perhaps to prevent further insertions, and that figure has been the benchmark since. In April 2025 the Gita manuscript was added to UNESCO's Memory of the World Register.

Persian translations were completed in the Mughal Empire in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. Charles Wilkins published the first English translation in 1785, with an introduction by Warren Hastings, and French (1787), German and Russian versions followed. Richard Davis cites a count of 1,891 translations in 75 languages by 1982.
sections.legacy:
In the modern age the Gita has served many causes. Neo-Hindus and Hindu nationalists took its emphasis on duty and action as a clue for their activism for Indian independence. Tilak wrote his commentary in jail in 1910 and 1911, and Vivekananda drew on the Gita for his lectures on the four yogas. Gandhi, who called it his 'spiritual dictionary', memorised the last 19 verses of chapter 2 and wrote a commentary in Gujarati in Yeravada jail in 1929. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada's Bhagavad-Gita as It Is is described as by far the most widely distributed English translation, and its publisher estimates sales at twenty-three million copies.

Readers have taken the battlefield as an allegory of the war within a person, as Vivekananda, Gandhi and Eknath Easwaran did, or as a real defence of the warrior's duty, as Steven Rosen, Laurie Patton and Stephen Mitchell do. It has also been criticised and defended on caste, since Krishna tells Arjuna to follow his sva-dharma, the duty of his varna, which Vivekananda read as the duty that comes with one's situation or profession.

Works of art drawn from it include Philip Glass's opera Satyagraha (1979), whose libretto consists of sayings from the Gita, and G. V. Iyer's Sanskrit film Bhagavad Gita (1993), which won the National Film Award for Best Film. J. Robert Oppenheimer recited a part of a verse from chapter 11 in a 1965 television documentary about the atomic bomb.

summary: The Bhagavad Gita is a Hindu scripture of 700 verses within the Mahabharata, a dialogue between Arjuna and Krishna before the Kurukshetra War. Tradition ascribes it to Vyasa; scholars see a composite work of the second or first century BCE, much commented on and translated.
references: Richard H. Davis, The 'Bhagavad Gita': A Biography (Princeton University Press, 2014)
Angelika Malinar, The Bhagavadgita (Cambridge University Press, 2007)
J.A.B. van Buitenen, The Bhagavadgita in the Mahabharata (University of Chicago Press, 2013)
Jeaneane D Fowler, The Bhagavad Gita: A Text and Commentary for Students (Sussex Academy Press, 2012)
Gavin Flood, The Bhagavad Gita: A New Translation (W.W. Norton & Company, 2013)
Franklin Edgerton, The Bhagavad Gita, Part 2 (Harvard University Press, 1952)
notes: Dating: the article gives 2nd or 1st century BCE as general, with 400-500 BCE, 5th/4th century BCE (Upadhyaya), 3rd century BCE or later (Basham), 300 BCE to 300 CE (Elgood) and 1st century CE estimates; start -200 follows the 'major revision' hint and the general range, with circa true. The article also says the first written version was probably 2nd or 3rd century CE (Sargeant), left out.

Internal tension: the article says Gambhirananda's 745-verse view is 'supported by' versions of Mahabharata 6.43 giving speaker counts of 574 + 84 + 41 + 1, which total 700, not 745. I left the speaker counts out and only report that old manuscripts 'may have had 745' and that none has been found.
The article gives the Gita as 6.25-42 or 6.23-40 in the full Mahabharata and as 6.3.23 to 6.3.40 in the manuscripts section; I used the first pair.

The article says Ramanuja lived in the 11th and early 12th centuries and heads his section 'c. 1100 CE'; the event uses c. 1100. Dnyaneshwar is given as 13th century, 1290 CE and 1275-1296; the event uses c. 1290.

Chapter 1's description says the epic and Krishna 'have already extolled ahimsa'; left out. Chapter titles and verse counts per chapter are in the article but not used beyond chapters 2, 3, 11, 12, 14 and 18.

Left out because contested or unattributed: the 'unlike any other religious scripture' claim about the battlefield, the 5,000-year-old claim in An Atheist Gets the Gita, and the 'most translated Asian text' claim (Minor), a comparative superlative.
Poem-genre note: the article says 'Hindu scripture' and calls it 'the most prominent sacred text' with pan-Hindu influence; I kept only Larson's attributed quotation to avoid a ranking.
The Oppenheimer line says 'a part of the verse'; I wrote 'a part of a verse' and did not quote it.
The article's Ganesha legend gives Ganesha as scribe of the Mahabharata 'along with the Bhagavad Gita'; kept as legend.
The article is thin on manuscripts' dates (no oldest manuscript named) and on the Gita's earliest reception before Shankara.
